newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudanese demonstrate against Ethiopia, Eritrea.
newsitem.headline: Sudanese demonstrate against Ethiopia, Eritrea.

text.p: Hundreds of Sudanese war volunteers staged a rally in downtown Khartoum on Monday to protest against what they called Eritrean and Ethiopian attacks along the borders of Africa's largest country.

The protesters, some dressed in camouflage fatigues and waving assault rifles in the air, were volunteers to the paramilitary People's Defence Force (PDF) who appeared to be answering last week's mobilisation call by President Omar Hassan al-Bashir.

Sudan says Ethiopia and Eritrea are behind attacks which began in the east of the country last week. A coalition of northern and southern opposition forces fighting to overthrow the Islamist government says it is responsible for the attacks.
Pedestrians along Baladiya street in the centre of the Sudanese capital stopped in their tracks to watch the convoy of six public transport buses packed with men and some women in war dress.
"Allahu Akbar (God is Greatest)," shouted groups of men in olive drab fatigues packed on top of the buses while pumping their fists in the air.
The buses pulled up alongside the office of the Administration for Provincial Coordination and their passengers spilled out. The streets swelled as curious passers-by stopped and pressed around them.
One Khartoum driver said that Baladiya street forks off in two directions which can be taken east to Kassala and south to the Blue Nile area.

Those are the spots where most of the fighting has been taking place. Sudanese rebels in Asmara said on Monday they had advanced to within 70 km (45 miles) of the Blue Nile capital Damazin, which supplies Khartoum with most of its electricity.
Some of the PDF fighters wore headbands and dark glasses, while others wore plastic sandles on their feet and were not dressed in fatigues or army gear.
The government has called on people to publicly protest against what it says are an Ethiopian and Eritrean invasion.

"This is the second time I am joining jihad (holy war)," said Somayya Mohammed, 21, a PDF volunteer. She was wearing fatigues under hejab, an Islamic style of dress that leaves only the face and hands uncovered.
She said she was joining the PDF because of the "call by Bashir and because we are Moslems".
Assila Amas, another young woman in hejab, said she was joining the PDF because of the "Ethiopian invasion on the eastern borders".
Hanan al-Zubeir, 25, who is a PDF coordinator, said "many women in all provinces of Sudan" had joined the force and that "all Sudanese women are participating in the process of jihad".
She said the women helped by preparing food or doing non-combat activities but asked if the women would take up arms, Zubeir said: "They are not fighting but they are ready."
